t: A Classroom Management Plan That Works
q: His point is that there is zero correlation between creative talent and the materials and equipment used.
There is no magic in the plan itself. It has no power to influence behavior. Only you have the power to influence behavior by creating a classroom your students want to be part of.
A classroom management plan is a contract you make with your students that promises you will protect their right to learn and enjoy school without interference.
The “do this and get that” mentality is a short-term solution that may get you through the day, and thus is a good strategy for substitute teachers, but it won’t actually change behavior.
Its usefulness comes from how it’s implemented, enforced, and carried out, from how you communicate with your students, from how much leverage you have with them.
Avoid cutesy and colorful designs. Even kindergarteners need to know that your classroom management plan and the rules by which it governs are sacred, serious.

t: 12 Classroom Management Myths You Need To Know About d-to-know-about/
q: Your smile should be the first thing students notice about you. It sets the tone for the new school year and gives you a jumpstart on building rapport.
Students will only take advantage of you if you say you’re going to hold them accountable and you don’t.
If students are having fun learning in your classroom, your rules and consequences will have more power to dissuade misbehavior.
Praising students for expected behavior sends the message that doing what you’re supposed to do deserves special recognition.
You don’t need tougher consequences. You just need to strengthen the ones you have. You do this by creating a classroom that students want to be a part of.
Sending students to the office weakens your ability to manage your classroom. It communicates to your students that the buck doesn’t stop with you.
You decide whether you have a good class or not, not the students. You have the power to create the class you want, regardless of who is on your roster.

t: How To Improve Classroom Management By Doing Less
q: If you slow down, move less, talk less, and at times do absolutely nothing, you will gain more control. And classroom management won’t be such a challenge.
It’s always smart to take your time. If you rush or get ahead of your students, you’ll lose them—and control of your class.
The reality is, the more you talk, the less your students will tune in and the more likely they are to misbehave.
If your students aren’t giving you what you want, stop whatever you’re doing. Stand in the most prominent place in the classroom (I like to stand on a chair) and do nothing.
When you raise your voice, you train your students to listen to you only when you get loud and to tune you out the other times.
More than any other area of teaching, effective classroom management requires you to work smarter, not harder.
x: Counterintuitively, doing less—slowing down, moving less, talking less—yields more classroom control than doing more.
Pause often when giving directions, allowing students time to process information and giving the teacher a chance to check comprehension.

t: How To Motivate Students Without Losing Control Of Your Class ntrol-of-your-class/
q: Students feed off of your energy, and excitability isn’t a good thing when it comes to classroom management. Yet, if your students are uninspired, then you’re not helping them grow academically.
You can certainly be calm on the inside while showing enthusiasm. But there are times when you need to show calm on the outside.
A high percentage of misbehavior occurs on the way in or on the way out of the classroom. So refrain from shuffling papers, talking to students, or making announcements.

Whenever you stand before your students to teach a lesson, you must show passion for your subject. To convince students that the subject you’re teaching is worthy of their attention, they have to see that you’re excited to teach it.
Reading great books aloud with gusto will motivate children to read better than any other method, technique, or strategy.
They get excited, stressed, and angry (enthusiasm of a different kind) when they should be calm and observant, and they become spiritless when they should be teaching like their hair is on fire.
x: Following the calm/enthusiasm guidelines improves classroom management, attentiveness, motivation, and students' love of school together.
Show genuine enthusiasm during lessons, modeling, read-alouds, storytelling, and learning games or experiments to build motivation.

Linsin addresses the tension between teacher enthusiasm, which motivates students, and calmness, which supports classroom control, arguing that effective teachers deploy both strategically like yin and yang.
